zh.q: 教材只给了用品和一张空表，这张表要怎么填？
zh.concl: 教材的做法是变量控制：一次只改一个条件、其余全相同，再用「出现浑浊的时间」或「收集 10 mL H₂ 的时间」把快慢变成可以比较的数。
points: 四站对应教材实验活动7 的三组对比，加一组教材图 2-1 的定量测定。
并排的两支管里总有一支是对照：只改一个条件的那支叫实验管。
读数栏把「看得见的现象」换成秒数，才比得出快几倍。

zh.q: 加了同样多的酸，为什么稀的那一支浑浊得更慢？
zh.concl: 其他条件相同时，减小反应物浓度，速率减小、时间变长：浓度减半，时间加倍（本课按一级关系设定，与教材的定性结论一致）。
points: 稀释那支另加 1 mL 蒸馏水，两管总体积都是 4 mL，只有浓度不同。
浓度按 0.1 mol/L × V / 4 mL 算出来，不是「看着稀一点」。
浑浊计时取「刚出现乳白」，两管用同一个标准才好比。

zh.q: 同一支管放进热水，为什么几乎立刻浑了？
zh.concl: 其他条件相同时，升高温度速率增大、降低温度速率减小；本课温度因子下每 10 ℃ 约 3 倍（教材给 2~4 倍），45 ℃ 时浑浊时间只有 25 ℃ 的约八分之一。
points: 两支管浓度相同（都是 2 mL 原管），唯一变量是水浴温度。
教材给「每升高 10 ℃ 速率增大为原来的 2~4 倍」；本课的温度因子每 10 ℃ 约 3 倍，落在区间里。
温度改的是「够能量的分子占多大比例」，不是把浓度改大。

zh.q: 只加一小撮黑色粉末，气泡为什么一下子密了？
zh.concl: 催化剂改变反应历程、降低活化能，使活化分子数目增大、单位时间有效碰撞次数增加，速率增大；它不改变反应热，也不改变平衡。
points: 三支管只有加入物不同，H₂O₂ 的体积与浓度都一样（各 2 mL 10%）。
空白管必须留着，否则「催化」这两个字就没了参照。
教材只说两种催化剂都比空白快、没比谁更快，所以本课给同一倍率，不排名次。

zh.concl: v = Δc/Δt：测出时间就能把快慢算成数；其他条件相同时，增大硫酸浓度速率增大（1 → 4 mol/L，时间由 64.0 s 缩到 16.0 s）。
points: 10 mL H₂ 在 25 ℃、101.325 kPa 下是 4.0876×10⁻⁴ mol，除以 40 mL 溶液得 Δc = 1.02×10⁻² mol/L。
速率用 H₂SO₄ 的浓度变化除以时间，单位 mol/(L·s)。
只收集 10 mL（反应刚开始的一小段），得到的是这一段的平均速率。

zh.q: 温度升高以后，瓶子里到底多了什么？
zh.concl: 浓度增大 → 单位体积内活化分子数增多；温度升高 → 活化分子百分数增大；催化剂降低活化能 → 更多分子成为活化分子。三者都让单位时间内有效碰撞次数增加，速率增大。
points: 分子撞在一起不等于反应：只有能量够、取向对的碰撞才有效。
温度升高不增加分子总数，增加的是「够能量的那部分」的比例。
催化剂不改分子能量，改的是门槛——活化能降下来，够能量的分子就多了。

zh.q: 两支管里的 Na₂S₂O₃ 不一样多、体积也不一样，这样比还公平吗？
zh.concl: 变量控制要求只改浓度、其余相同：稀释管必须补 1 mL 蒸馏水保持总体积 4 mL，否则浓度算错、计时偏短，比出来的差别被压缩。
points: 错误操作 → 总体积只有 3 mL → c 由 0.025 变 0.0333 → 浑浊时间由 40.0 s 变 30.0 s（偏小）→ 结论被削弱。
计时标准要一致：看「刚出现浑浊」还是「完全浑浊」，时间能差一半。
温度没回到室温就换管比较，也属于没控制变量。

zh.q: 考核：把教材的浓度对照实验完整复现一遍
zh.concl: 考核没有新结论：把「1 mL + 1 mL 水、总体积 4 mL、25 ℃」三件事同时照顾到，浑浊时间才落在 40.0 s 附近。
points: 不补水时间会偏到 30.0 s，差 10.0 s 就出界。
水浴被抬到 45 ℃，时间就从 40.0 s 掉到 2.4 s，比浓度的影响还大。
计时标准要前后一致：两管都取「刚出现乳白」。

en.q: The textbook only gives the materials and an empty table. How do you fill it in?
en.concl: The textbook's method is variable control: change one condition at a time and keep everything else the same, then use "time for cloudiness" or "time to collect 10 mL H₂" to turn speed into a comparable number.
points: The four stations match the three comparisons of textbook Lab Activity 7, plus the quantitative measurement of textbook Fig. 2-1.
Of each pair of tubes, one is always the control; the one with a single condition changed is the experimental tube.
The reading bar turns "what you see" into seconds, so you can say how many times faster.

en.q: With the same amount of acid, why does the dilute tube cloud more slowly?
en.concl: With other conditions the same, lower reactant concentration means a slower rate and longer time: half the concentration, double the time (this lesson assumes a first-order relation, consistent with the textbook's qualitative conclusion).
points: The diluted tube gets 1 mL extra distilled water, so both tubes have 4 mL in total and only the concentration differs.
The concentration is calculated as 0.1 mol/L × V / 4 mL, not "looks a bit weaker".
Cloudiness is timed at "milkiness just appears"; both tubes must use the same criterion to compare.

en.q: Put the same tube in hot water: why does it cloud almost at once?
en.concl: With other conditions the same, raising the temperature speeds up the rate and lowering it slows it down; with this lesson's factor of about 3 per 10 ℃ (textbook 2–4), the cloudiness time at 45 ℃ is only about one eighth of that at 25 ℃.
points: Both tubes have the same concentration (both 2 mL original); the only variable is the bath temperature.
The textbook says "each 10 ℃ rise multiplies the rate by 2–4"; this lesson's temperature factor is about 3 per 10 ℃, within that range.
Temperature changes "what fraction of molecules have enough energy", not the concentration.

en.q: Why do the bubbles suddenly thicken after adding just a pinch of black powder?
en.concl: A catalyst changes the reaction pathway and lowers the activation energy, increasing the number of activated molecules and effective collisions per unit time, so the rate increases; it changes neither the heat of reaction nor the equilibrium.
points: The three tubes differ only in what is added; the volume and concentration of H₂O₂ are the same (2 mL of 10% each).
The blank tube must stay, or "catalysis" has nothing to compare with.
The textbook only says both catalysts are faster than the blank, not which is faster, so this lesson gives them the same factor and does not rank them.

en.q: Can "fast or slow" become a number?
en.concl: v = Δc/Δt: measuring the time turns speed into a number; with other conditions the same, a higher acid concentration gives a faster rate (1 → 4 mol/L, time cut from 64.0 s to 16.0 s).
points: mL of H₂ at 25 ℃ and 101.325 kPa is 4.0876×10⁻⁴ mol; divided by 40 mL of solution, Δc = 1.02×10⁻² mol/L.
The rate is the change in H₂SO₄ concentration divided by time, in mol/(L·s).
Only 10 mL is collected (a short stretch at the start), so this gives the average rate over that stretch.

en.q: After heating, what is there more of in the flask?
en.concl: Higher concentration → more activated molecules per unit volume; higher temperature → larger percentage of activated molecules; a catalyst lowers the activation energy → more molecules become activated. All three increase the effective collisions per unit time and speed up the rate.
points: Molecules colliding is not the same as reacting: only collisions with enough energy and the right orientation are effective.
Raising the temperature does not add molecules; it raises the fraction "with enough energy".
A catalyst doesn't change molecular energy, it changes the threshold: with a lower activation energy, more molecules have enough energy.

en.q: The two tubes hold different amounts of Na₂S₂O₃ and different volumes. Is that a fair comparison?
en.concl: Variable control requires changing only the concentration and keeping the rest the same: the diluted tube must be topped up with 1 mL distilled water to keep 4 mL in total, or the concentration is miscalculated, the time is too short, and the measured difference is squeezed.
points: Wrong procedure → total volume only 3 mL → c from 0.025 to 0.0333 → cloudiness time from 40.0 s to 30.0 s (too short) → the conclusion is weakened.
The timing criterion must be consistent: "cloudiness just appears" versus "fully cloudy" can differ by half.
Swapping tubes before the temperature is back to room temperature also fails to control variables.

en.q: Assessment: reproduce the textbook's concentration control experiment in full
en.concl: The assessment has no new conclusion: only with "1 mL + 1 mL water, 4 mL in total, 25 ℃" all looked after at once does the cloudiness time land near 40.0 s.
points: Without the top-up the time drifts to 30.0 s, 10.0 s off and out of range.
When the bath is raised to 45 ℃ the time drops from 40.0 s to 2.4 s, an even bigger effect than concentration.
The timing criterion must be consistent: take "milkiness just appears" for both tubes.
